title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E506 re-derives Lagrange's integration of dx/√X = dy/√Y, where X = A+Bx+Cx²+Dx³+Ex⁴ and Y is the same quartic in y. In §46 Euler recalls an earlier form of the complete integral, (M√Y + N√X)/(x−y)³ = const, with explicit polynomials M and N. On this page he first records the symmetric combinations:

M+N = 8A + 4B(x+y) + 2C(x+y)² + D(x+y)³ + 4Exy(x²+y²),
M−N = (x−y)[2B + 2C(x+y) + D(x²+4xy+y²) + 4Exy(x+y)].

These are meant to show how the form relates to the symmetric, rationalised integral of §44–45, the 'canonical equation' α + 2β(x+y) + γ(x²+y²) + 2δxy + 2εxy(x+y) + ζx²y² = 0. Euler admits it is 'not easily understood' how the two forms agree, although agreement is certain.

§47: because the arbitrary constant can be written in endlessly many ways, he fixes a normalisation. Choose the integral so that y=0 gives x=k, and hence X=K with K = A+Bk+Ck²+Dk³+Ek⁴. In modern terms, x is the 'sum' of y and k under the addition law, with base point 0 as the neutral element. With this rule all integrals can be brought into full agreement.

§48, Theorem I: for dx/(a+bx+cx²) = dy/(a+by+cy²), the normalised integral is (2a + b(x+y) + 2cxy)/(x−y) = (2a+bk)/k. This is the bilinear (Möbius) addition law attached to a quadratic. It follows the Riccati-type, tan/tanh-type pattern on the projective line, i.e. a one-dimensional algebraic group (additive or multiplicative/torus type, depending on the discriminant). Theorems II–III on the next page continue the list: the + sign case, then the square-root (conic) case.
errors: The formula for M−N has a misprinted parenthesis: '4Exy(x+y(x−y)' should read 4Exy(x+y)(x−y).
No mathematical errors. M+N and M−N check out by direct expansion. For example, D[x²(x+3y) − y²(y+3x)] = D(x−y)(x²+4xy+y²).
Theorem I checks in the special cases a only (x−y constant) and c only (1/y − 1/x constant), and in general as a Möbius invariant. The normalisation degenerates at k=0 (the identity).

ideas.what: Decomposing M±N for the integral (M√Y+N√X)/(x−y)³ = C
ideas.modern_name: Symmetric/antisymmetric decomposition of an addition-theorem invariant
ideas.where_published: E506 itself; the M,N form is from earlier sections of E506 (§8)

ideas.what: Normalising the arbitrary constant so that y=0 gives x=k
ideas.modern_name: Choice of neutral element/base point in the addition law (x = y ⊕ k)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (the 'lex compositionis' of his elliptic addition papers)
ideas.where_published: Euler's addition-theorem papers of the 1750s–60s (e.g. E251, E261) and Institutiones calculi integralis I; recurring normalisation

ideas.what: Integral of dx/(a+bx+cx²) = dy/(a+by+cy²) in the form (2a+b(x+y)+2cxy)/(x−y) = (2a+bk)/k
ideas.modern_name: Möbius/bilinear addition law for a quadratic differential (one-dimensional algebraic group law)
ideas.where_published: Euler's integral calculus treatments of separated Riccati-type equations; standard

missed.claim: Euler explicitly leaves unshown the algebraic equivalence between the (M√Y+N√X)/(x−y)³ form and the Lagrange-derived rationalised canonical form. It is a routine elimination, so its significance is minimal.
missed.quote: Interim tamen haud facile intelligitur, quomodo haec forma cum ante inuenta consentiat, dum tamen de consensu certi esse possumus.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as a historical note. Verification is straightforward with modern algebra: square to remove the radicals and compare with the biquadratic form.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine: algebraic bookkeeping, a standard normalisation of the integration constant, and the well-known bilinear addition law for the quadratic case. Nothing appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Image reads 'K = ·+ A + Bk + Ckk + Dk³ + Ek⁴' (stray dot); the transcription 'K = + A ...' is fine.
The misprint '4Exy(x+y(x−y)' is faithful to the original; intended 4Exy(x+y)(x−y).
